meta.description: Not a Thoreau original. This rose-and-thorns proverb was in print by 1809, before Thoreau was born; Wikiquote lists it as misattributed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Truths and roses have thorns about them'?
meta.ogDescription: It predates Thoreau. An anonymous proverb documented in print in 1809 — he copied it into his journal, he did not coin it.

answer.label: Not original to Thoreau — an older proverb
answer.authorDates: Attested in print by 1809 · anonymous English aphorism, older than Thoreau
answer.sourceLine: “Truths and roses have thorns about them” is an anonymous aphorism that was already in print before Thoreau was born in 1817. He is said to have copied it into his journal on 14 June 1838, but Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗ for exactly that reason — he recorded the proverb rather than coining it, and it does not appear in his standard published Journal.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: Truths and roses have thorns about them
An anonymous English proverb, in print by 1809 — before Thoreau's birth
Said to have copied it into his journal, 14 June 1838 (per Wikiquote) — transcribed, not coined

source.excerpt: Truths and roses have thorns about them.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its Misattributed section, noting Thoreau “wrote it in his journal… but it was not original.”
Wikiquote traces it in print to Joseph Dennie & Asbury Dickins, The Port Folio (July 1809), p. 431 ↗ — eight years before Thoreau was born.
The standard 1906 published Journal, Vol. 1 ↗ does not print this sentence, so the popular “Thoreau said it” framing rests on a copied maxim at best.
Quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ credit Thoreau with no source at all.
source.excerptNote: The line circulated as a stand-alone proverb; no larger original passage by Thoreau is known, and it is absent from his published Journal, Vol. 1.
source.rightsNote: The wording is an anonymous English aphorism documented in print by 1809 — more than a century before the 1931 U.S. copyright cutoff — so the phrase itself is firmly in the public domain.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: Henry David Thoreau
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was the Concord essayist and naturalist behind Walden and Civil Disobedience. From 1837 he kept voluminous journals that mixed original reflection with copied maxims and reading notes. This rose-and-thorns line reads like one of those borrowed proverbs; its fame as a “Thoreau quote” comes from later quote collectors, not from anything he claimed as his own invention.

cite.sourceCitation: Attributed to Henry David Thoreau but not original to him; documented in print before his birth, e.g. in Joseph Dennie and Asbury Dickins, The Port Folio, vol. 2, no. 1 (Philadelphia, July 1809), 431, as cited in Wikiquote.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Thoreau
misattribution.intro: The sentiment is genuine and the line is old — but the “Henry David Thoreau” byline is the modern quote-industry's doing, not history's.

items.why: Thoreau is said to have jotted the proverb into his journal (14 June 1838), and later anthologists turned that transcription into a “Thoreau quote.” Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed for exactly this reason: he copied it, he did not coin it.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a traditional aphorism that predates Thoreau — already in print in The Port Folio (1809) ↗ and in a Spanish-language exercise book (1811) ↗ — both before his birth in 1817.

context.heading: What it means
lead: Truths and roses have thorns about them is a compact paradox: the things most worth having — honest truth, real beauty — come guarded by something that pricks. A rose defends its bloom with thorns; a truth defends itself by being uncomfortable to hold.
As folk wisdom it belongs to a whole family of rose-and-thorn maxims, and its survival owes more to that proverbial tradition than to any single author.
context.pull: The best things come guarded — the rose by its thorn, the truth by its sting.
